content: 1. Magnesium citrate can decrease the levels of deferiprone by enhancing gastrointestinal (GI) absorption. This interaction is relevant only when both agents are administered orally. Close monitoring is recommended. Deferiprone may also bind to polyvalent cations (e.g., iron, aluminum, zinc), so administration should be separated by at least 4 hours from other medications or supplements containing these cations, such as antacids. 2. Both magnesium citrate and deflazacort can lower serum potassium levels. Caution is advised, and close monitoring is necessary. 3. Magnesium citrate reduces the levels of demeclocycline by inhibiting its GI absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. It is recommended to avoid this combination or use an alternative drug. 4. Dextrose can decrease magnesium citrate levels by increasing renal clearance. This interaction is considered minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 5. Digoxin can reduce magnesium citrate levels by increasing renal clearance. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 6. Magnesium citrate decreases the levels or effects of dolutegravir by binding to cations in the GI tract. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. It is recommended to avoid this combination or use an alternative drug. If co-administration is necessary, dolutegravir should be taken 2 hours before or 6 hours after magnesium citrate. 7. Doxercalciferol can increase magnesium citrate levels by enhancing GI absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. The clinical significance is unknown. 8. Magnesium citrate reduces doxycycline levels by inhibiting GI absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. Avoid this combination or use an alternative drug. 9. Drospirenone increases magnesium citrate levels by decreasing renal clearance. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 10. Magnesium citrate decreases eltrombopag levels by inhibiting GI absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. This combination is contraindicated, and administration should be separated by at least 4 hours. 11. Estradiol decreases magnesium citrate levels by shifting magnesium from the blood to tissue storage. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 12. Conjugated synthetic estrogens decrease magnesium citrate levels by shifting magnesium from the blood to tissue storage. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 13. Esterified estrogens decrease magnesium citrate levels by shifting magnesium from the blood to tissue storage. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 14. Estropipate decreases magnesium citrate levels by shifting magnesium from the blood to tissue storage. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 15. Ethacrynic acid decreases magnesium citrate levels by increasing renal clearance. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 16. Magnesium citrate reduces fleroxacin levels by inhibiting GI absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. Caution is advised, and administration should be separated by 2 hours. 17. Furosemide decreases magnesium citrate levels by increasing renal clearance. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 18. Magnesium citrate reduces gemifloxacin levels by inhibiting GI absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. Caution is advised, and administration should be separated by 2 hours. 19. Gentamicin decreases magnesium citrate levels by increasing renal clearance. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 20. Intranasal glucagon increases magnesium citrate levels by decreasing renal clearance. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 21. Hydrochlorothiazide decreases magnesium citrate levels by increasing renal clearance. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 22. Magnesium citrate reduces ibandronate levels by inhibiting GI absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. The clinical significance is unknown. 23. Ifosfamide and magnesium citrate can increase each other's toxicity through nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. Therapy modification and close monitoring of electrolytes and renal function are recommended. 24. Indapamide decreases magnesium citrate levels by increasing renal clearance. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 25. Magnesium citrate reduces levofloxacin levels by inhibiting GI absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. Caution is advised, and administration should be separated by 2 hours. 26. Mannitol decreases magnesium citrate levels by increasing renal clearance. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 27. Mestranol decreases magnesium citrate levels by shifting magnesium from the blood to tissue storage. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 28. Methyclothiazide decreases magnesium citrate levels by increasing renal clearance. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 29. Metolazone decreases magnesium citrate levels by increasing renal clearance. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 30. Magnesium citrate reduces minocycline levels by inhibiting GI absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. Avoid this combination or use an alternative drug. 31. Magnesium citrate reduces moxifloxacin levels by inhibiting GI absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. Caution is advised, and administration should be separated by 2 hours. 32. Oral neomycin decreases magnesium citrate levels by increasing renal clearance. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 33. Magnesium citrate reduces nitrofurantoin levels by inhibiting GI absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. The clinical significance is unknown. 34. Magnesium citrate reduces ofloxacin levels by inhibiting GI absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. Caution is advised, and administration should be separated by 2 hours. 35. Magnesium citrate reduces omadacycline levels by inhibiting GI absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. Therapy modification and close monitoring are recommended. 36. Multivalent cation-containing products may impair the absorption of tetracyclines, reducing their efficacy. Dosing of tetracyclines should be separated from these products. 37. Magnesium citrate reduces oxytetracycline levels by inhibiting GI absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. Avoid this combination or use an alternative drug. 38. Paromomycin decreases magnesium citrate levels by increasing renal clearance. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 39. Magnesium citrate reduces penicillamine levels by inhibiting GI absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. Caution is advised, and administration should be separated by 2 hours. 40. Magnesium citrate reduces the effects of potassium phosphates (IV) by cation binding in the GI tract. Avoid this combination or use an alternative drug. Magnesium also decreases serum phosphate concentrations by binding dietary phosphate. 41. Magnesium citrate reduces sarecycline levels by inhibiting GI absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. Therapy modification and close monitoring are recommended. 42. Magnesium citrate reduces the effects of sodium phosphates (IV) by cation binding in the GI tract. Therapy modification and close monitoring are recommended. Magnesium also decreases serum phosphate concentrations by binding dietary phosphate. 43. Sodium polystyrene sulfonate increases magnesium citrate levels by decreasing renal clearance. This interaction is minor, but there is a risk of alkalosis. 44. Spironolactone increases magnesium citrate levels by decreasing renal clearance. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 45. Streptomycin decreases magnesium citrate levels by increasing renal clearance. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 46. Magnesium citrate reduces tetracycline levels by inhibiting GI absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. Avoid this combination or use an alternative drug. 47. Tobramycin decreases magnesium citrate levels by increasing renal clearance. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 48. Torsemide decreases magnesium citrate levels by increasing renal clearance. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 49. Triamterene increases magnesium citrate levels by decreasing renal clearance. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 50. Vitamin D increases magnesium citrate levels by other mechanisms, particularly in the presence of renal impairment. The combined use of vitamin D and magnesium-containing products should be avoided in patients with chronic renal failure. 51. Magnesium citrate is associated with potential adverse effects, including abdominal cramping, diarrhea, electrolyte imbalance, hypermagnesemia, gas formation, nausea, and vomiting. It should only be used occasionally for constipation treatment, as prolonged use may lead to serious adverse effects. 52. Magnesium citrate should be used under physician supervision in patients with sodium or magnesium-restricted diets, kidney dysfunction, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, or sudden changes in bowel habits persisting for over 2 weeks. Caution is advised in patients with myasthenia gravis or other neuromuscular diseases. 53. Magnesium citrate is contraindicated in renal failure, existing electrolyte imbalance, appendicitis, acute surgical abdomen, myocardial damage, heart block, fecal impaction, rectal fissures, intestinal obstruction, perforation, or dehydration. Discontinue use and consult a healthcare provider if bowel movement does not occur or rectal bleeding develops. 54. Magnesium citrate is classified as Pregnancy Category A, indicating it is generally acceptable for use during pregnancy. Controlled studies in pregnant women show no evidence of fetal risk. Its use in nursing mothers appears to be safe.
